title: Exercise: Build-a-Chart
text:
In this exercise you won’t draw a chart from scratch. Instead, you’ll choose a story and then stack ready-made layers in Miro to build the chart that tells it. Every choice is a design decision, and you should be ready to explain why you made it.
There’s more than one right answer, and a few wrong ones.

title: Exercise: Build-a-Chart
text:
How it works

Pick a story. Read the data below with your partner and finish this sentence: “The story I want to tell is…”
Build it. In the Miro board, stack one layer for each design decision on your build frame.
Justify it. Add a sticky note next to your chart explaining why you chose each layer.
Review. Swap with another pair and evaluate their chart using the checklist. Find at least one strength and one thing to fix.







TipBuilding tips




Choose your measure first. The chart layers are grouped by measure: pick from the dollars drawer or the percent drawer, so your data matches your axis.
Chart type and color come as one layer. Find the row for your chart type and the column for your color.
Line up each layer. Every layer is 1600 × 1000. Set its width and height to match, and give it the same X/Y position as your build frame.

title: Exercise: Build-a-Chart
text:
Questions to discuss

Does your measure match your story? When does a percent tell a different story than a dollar amount?
Does your chart type fit what you want to show: a part-to-whole, or a change over time?
Does every use of color have a reason? Would your chart work for a colorblind reader, or in grayscale?
Can a reader understand your chart without looking back and forth to a legend?
Can someone state your main takeaway in 5 seconds from the title?
Is your chart honest? Think about what “current dollars” means over ten years.

See the companion guide for the practices behind each decision.

title: Visualize It: Designing Impactful and Accessible Data Visualizations
text: Data visualization is essential in library work, yet few practitioners receive formal training in it. This workshop equips library professionals at any level with a practical foundation in the design of accessible and effective data visualizations, combining theory with hands-on practice, leaving participants with a framework they can immediately apply.

title: Visualize It: Designing Impactful and Accessible Data Visualizations
text:
Learning outcomes
After completing this workshop, attendees will be able to:

Explain how principles of visual perception inform effective data visualization design.
Evaluate a data visualization by identifying specific design and accessibility strengths and weaknesses using a structured framework.
Apply design principles, such as color selection, typography, labeling, and accessibility guidelines to revise a data visualization for clarity and impact.

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
1. Know your message

Find your story. Decide what you want the reader to learn before you choose a chart.
Match the chart to the story. Visit the Data Viz Catalogue for help choosing the right visualization for what you want to show. Some examples:

Comparison: bar chart
Trend over time: line chart
Part-to-whole: stacked bar chart, donut chart or pie chart (best with five or fewer categories)

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
2. Keep it simple and clear

Remove “chart-junk.” Delete unnecessary borders, backgrounds, gridlines, and 3D effects. If an element can be removed without losing information, remove it.
Label everything, or explain it in the caption. This includes axis labels (with units), legends, and the data source.
Make text readable. Use fonts large enough to read when printed or displayed.
Order categories meaningfully. Sort bars by value rather than alphabetically, unless there is a natural order such as time or age group.
Use direct labeling when possible. Label lines and bars directly instead of making readers look back and forth to a legend. If you must use a legend, order it to match the order of the data.
Split complex charts into several smaller charts, one for each value of a variable. For example, instead of using color to show five regions in one chart, make one panel per region (also called facets or trellis plots). Use the same axes in every panel so they’re easy to compare.

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
3. Use color with purpose

Every use of color needs a reason. Color should highlight data, or represent values, not decorate.
Limit categorical colors to six. If you need more, collapse categories into groups or simplify to a single muted color plus one highlight accent.
Keep colors consistent across charts. If “Region: Midwest” is blue on one chart, it should be blue on all other charts.
Avoid rainbow palettes for quantitative information. They create false boundaries and are hard to put in order.
Tip: View your chart in grayscale. Is it still understandable?

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
4. Make it accessible

Check contrast (WCAG 2.1 AA). Chart elements need at least 3:1 and text needs at least 4.5:1. Verify at webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker.
Choose colorblind-friendly palettes. Examples (not exhaustive):

Categorical: Okabe-Ito
Continuous: Viridis
Diverging: blue–red or blue–orange

Test your chart. Use the Coblis color blindness simulator to see how your image looks with different types of color vision deficiency: color-blindness.com/coblis-color-blindness-simulator.
Write alt-text.

Simple plots: a short summary plus a data table.
Complex plots: a short summary plus a long description.

Never rely on color alone to convey meaning.

Use redundant codings, e.g., color and marker shape in a scatterplot.

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
5. Be honest

Be careful with axis ranges. Bar charts should start at zero because bar length encodes the value. Line and scatter charts can use a non-zero baseline when it is clearly labeled.
Don’t use axis breaks. If outliers compress your data, use a clearly labeled logarithmic scale or add a separate zoomed-in panel.
Show uncertainty (error bars, confidence intervals) when it matters.
Cite your data source and note any exclusions or transformations.

title: Data Visualization Recommended Practices
text:
6. A quick checklist


Can someone state the main takeaway in 5 seconds?
Is everything labeled that will not be explained in a caption?
Is anything on the chart removable without losing information?
Does it work in grayscale and for colorblind readers?
Does it pass contrast checks?
Does it have alt-text?
Did someone unfamiliar with the data review it?
